title.rendered: Tinubu’s state police push: Security solution or 2027 political strategy?

content.rendered:
As the National Assembly moves to create state police with the recent passage of the bill seeking to establish the formations across the country, Nigeria finds itself at a critical crossroads. While advocates hail the proposal as a bold step towards tackling insecurity through true federalism, opponents fear it could hand governors a powerful political tool capable of undermining democracy ahead of the 2027 elections. DARE AKOGUN examines the competing arguments, the constitutional hurdles, lessons from other federations, and whether President Bola Tinubu’s security gamble will strengthen national security or deepen political tensions

The Senate’s recent passage of the Constitution Alteration Bill seeking to establish state police has reignited one of Nigeria’s longest-running constitutional debates, exposing deep divisions over whether decentralised policing is the long-awaited solution to the country’s worsening insecurity or a dangerous political weapon that could be abused ahead of the 2027 general election.

While supporters describe the proposal as a historic step towards true federalism and community policing, critics argue that the timing raises troubling questions about political motives, especially as preparations for the next election cycle gather momentum.

The sharp disagreements, coming barely days after the National Assembly approved the amendment, have once again placed the spotlight on Nigeria’s decades-old struggle to balance national security with democratic accountability.

For years, successive administrations have acknowledged that Nigeria’s highly centralised policing structure is overstretched and increasingly incapable of responding effectively to terrorism, kidnapping, banditry, communal violence, and organised crime.

With one police force serving more than 230 million people, security experts have repeatedly argued that officers deployed from Abuja often lack adequate knowledge of local terrain, language, culture, and community dynamics necessary for effective intelligence gathering.

The proposed constitutional amendment seeks to change that by allowing states to establish their own police commands while retaining the Nigeria Police Force as the federal policing institution.

Yet, despite widespread acceptance that policing requires reform, consensus on state police remains elusive.

Opposition fears political manipulation

Leading the opposition against immediate implementation is the People’s Redemption Party, which openly questioned the Federal Government’s credibility to oversee such a far-reaching constitutional reform.

The party argued that although Nigeria urgently requires security reforms, the current administration has not demonstrated sufficient competence to manage existing security institutions.

“The APC administration has failed to manage our security structure and institutions. Its plan to engineer the emergence of state police is suspicious and should be rejected,” the party stated.

The PRP further argued that President Bola Tinubu’s administration lacks the moral authority to implement a reform capable of fundamentally altering Nigeria’s security architecture before first earning greater public confidence through credible governance.

According to the party, Nigerians should first assess the administration’s democratic credentials during the next general election before entrusting it with state policing.

Similarly, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar’s camp questioned the urgency surrounding the legislation.

Speaking on Arise Television, Atiku’s media adviser, Paul Ibe, insisted that although the former vice-president supports state policing in principle, introducing it shortly before the 2027 elections could create opportunities for abuse.

“What Atiku Abubakar will not do in an election year is to ramp up legislation for state police because what they are trying to do is to sign this into law and give state governors that they have coerced into their party, the APC, the opportunity to recruit the thugs associated with them for the 2027 election,” Ibe alleged.

He maintained that the opposition’s concern was not about decentralised policing itself but about the timing of its implementation.

“We support state police, but not at this time. Why don’t they focus on critical issues? Why don’t they boost security in vulnerable communities?” he asked.

Peter Obi urges a delay

Adding another dimension to the debate, Labour Party presidential candidate Peter Obi also urged President Tinubu to postpone implementation until after the 2027 elections.

Although Obi acknowledged that state policing aligns with longstanding calls for restructuring, he warned that introducing it under the present political climate could undermine public confidence.

“The recent passage of the State Police Bill marks a significant legislative milestone,” Obi said.

“For years, many of us have consistently argued that a highly centralised policing structure is fundamentally unsuitable for Nigeria.”

However, he argued that implementation raises “legitimate concerns.”

According to Obi, the Federal Government should first establish strong safeguards, including an independent State Police Service Commission insulated from governors’ direct control.

“There is no guarantee that this administration can resist the temptation to take advantage of state policing to influence the 2027 general election by proxy.

“In view of that possibility and the danger it poses to the polity, it is necessary to defer its implementation until after the general election,” Obi stated.

Falana: State police alone won’t solve insecurity

Human rights lawyer Femi Falana, SAN, believes the debate itself misses the bigger picture.

Appearing on Channels Television’s Politics Today, Falana argued that security reforms must go beyond establishing additional police institutions.

According to him, unemployment, poverty, and poor social welfare remain major drivers of insecurity.

“The debates have been on since we started the campaign for restructuring.

“How do we employ more policemen without considering social security?

“Why are we not talking about creating employment for young people?

“And unless you address this problem holistically, creating state police or local government police will not address the crisis of insecurity,” Falana said.

His intervention reflects growing concerns among governance experts that security cannot be separated from economic realities.

Funding concerns remain

President of the Yoruba Ronu Leadership Forum, Akin Malaolu, welcomed the conversation but warned against presenting state police as a miracle solution.

According to him, decentralisation alone cannot cure structural weaknesses affecting Nigeria’s security institutions.

He also questioned whether financially struggling states possess the capacity to establish and sustain effective police organisations.

Malaolu advocated a comprehensive review of Nigeria’s revenue allocation formula before implementation.

He further warned that overlapping responsibilities between federal and state police formations could trigger operational conflicts if constitutional responsibilities are not clearly defined.

“Without addressing the structural weaknesses of the existing system, decentralising policing may simply multiply existing challenges,” he said.

Supporters see historic breakthrough

Despite the reservations, support for state police continues to grow.

Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu described the Senate’s action as “epochal,” congratulating President Tinubu for advancing a reform he had consistently championed during his tenure as Lagos governor.

According to him, decentralised policing represents a major milestone in Nigeria’s democratic evolution and the fight against insecurity.

Pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation Afenifere also praised both the President and the National Assembly, urging state Houses of Assembly to expedite ratification once the amendment reaches them.

The group advised governors to recruit competent personnel, provide modern equipment, and guarantee adequate welfare packages for future officers.

The Labour Party equally endorsed the legislation despite concerns over possible abuse.

The party argued that constitutional safeguards incorporated into the amendment would minimise political interference while strengthening community policing.

The Conference of Speakers of State Legislatures also backed the proposal.

Its Chairman, Emomotimi Dennis Guwor, said community-based policing would improve intelligence gathering because officers familiar with local language, culture, and terrain are better positioned to prevent crime.

Former Senator Gbenga Ashafa similarly welcomed the development but stressed that funding, command structure, and operational jurisdiction must be carefully resolved before implementation begins.

Road ahead

Although the Senate has passed the amendment, the process is far from complete.

The proposal still requires approval by at least 24 State Houses of Assembly before it can receive presidential assent.

That stage may prove equally contentious as state lawmakers, civil society groups, security experts, and political actors scrutinize the details of the proposed policing framework.

For many Nigerians, the debate goes beyond policing.

It raises broader questions about restructuring, federalism, democratic accountability, and whether constitutional reforms introduced close to a major election can be insulated from political interests.

Whether state police eventually become Nigeria’s most significant security reform in decades or another divisive constitutional experiment may ultimately depend less on the law itself than on the safeguards put in place to ensure that policing serves citizens rather than politicians.
